title: Track reference chains
summary: Resolve pronouns, demonstratives and descriptive phrases by linking each expression to a precise earlier person, object, action or result.

sections.title: Follow the repeated idea
content: Writers avoid repeating the same noun in every sentence. They use pronouns such as he, they and it; demonstratives such as this and that; and descriptive phrases such as the device or the first group.
Read two linked sentences. Underline the expression that points backward, then draw an arrow to the exact word, action or result it replaces.

sections.title: Use Locate, Match and Substitute
content: Locate: find the reference expression and read the complete sentence containing it.

Match: scan backward for candidates that agree in number, person and meaning. A plural pronoun needs a plural referent; a phrase such as this decision usually points to an action or choice rather than a person.
Substitute: replace the reference expression with your candidate and reread the sentence. Keep the candidate only if the sentence remains grammatical and logical.
When several nouns appear nearby, meaning controls the answer. The nearest noun is only a candidate, not an automatic answer.

sections.title: Resolve a chain, not one isolated word
content: Example: “Maya showed Idris the cracked sensor. He photographed it before returning the device to the laboratory.” The human pronoun he refers to Idris, the object pronoun it refers to the cracked sensor, and the descriptive phrase the device continues the same sensor reference.
Test each link separately. Idris matches he in person and number. The sensor matches it in number and meaning. Calling the sensor the device is also sensible in the final action.
A chain can cross a sentence or paragraph boundary, so keep a short list of active people, objects and results while reading.

sections.title: Name the whole referent
content: For a pronoun, name the precise person or thing. For a phrase such as this change or that finding, restate the complete earlier action or result rather than copying only one nearby noun.
Use a three-column note: reference expression, possible anchors, proof. Cross out candidates that fail agreement or make the sentence illogical.

sections.title: Trace references across paragraphs
content: Build a brief passage map first, then follow each reference backward to its anchor. A later phrase may depend on an earlier label such as the first group, so preserve those labels in your map.
Answer with the smallest complete referent. Include enough detail to identify the intended action or result, but do not copy an entire paragraph.

sections.title: Diagnose a broken reference link
content: Nearest-noun trap: I chose the closest noun without testing meaning.
Agreement mismatch: my answer did not match the reference in number or person.
Incomplete event: I named one noun when this or that referred to a whole action or result.
Lost chain: I forgot how a label in an earlier paragraph was reused later. Record the cause before correcting the answer.

sections.title: The mangrove nursery experiment
content: Trace six reference links in one original five-paragraph passage. All responses are marked together so feedback from an early item cannot reveal a later answer.
